metadata.projectName: Aamako Maya (आमाको माया — "Mother's Love") — mother-facing app, toll-free midwife counselling service, FCHV/ANM field tool, and a national DHIS2-based counselling programme
metadata.author: Amakomaya

sections.gov_regulatory: Non-clinical wellness tool today — the app makes no diagnostic/treatment claim and danger-sign triage is done by a human ANM, not software. This is live, not fixed: three risk scores (PRAMS, SORS, WHO Risk Score) are already collected in DHIS2, and switching on automated triage against them is named as the organisation's highest-value next act — which would reopen the classification question toward Class IIa clinical decision support. Named gap: Nepal has no regulatory sandbox or SaMD classification framework, and no ISO 13485/IEC 62304/ISO 14971 certification is evidenced.
sections.gov_clinical: Danger signs are triaged by a human on the counselling line, not automatically, because automated detection without a referral pathway is judged unsafe; the same logic has kept mental-health screening and automated risk-score triage switched off. Named gap: no single national maternal/newborn protocol repository to cite as 'the governing protocol' (no PNPK-equivalent in Nepal), and no adverse-event/near-miss reporting pathway is evidenced in the organisation's own records.
sections.gov_data: Stated policy: mother data is available only to the DHO, Government of Nepal, and the related health post/management — never publicly available, treated as a founding value. Named gap: Nepal's closest law is the general Individual Privacy Act, 2075 (2018); there is no health-sector-specific data protection law, so this commitment currently rests on internal policy, not a health-data statute. Consent-capture process and end-of-project data fate are not formally documented and are named as open items.
sections.gov_tech: The counselling programme runs on the national DHIS2-based platform (19,699 enrolled, 160 data elements, 27 indicators), not a standalone database, with a four-tier access model (mother/FCHV/health post/DHO) and scoped third-party access for at least one partner. The organisation separately holds FHIR R5 work (16 profiles, hmis.gov.np/fhir) at company level, but this product's own consumption of it is not evidenced. Offline-first by design (historically micro-SD/shared-device distribution). Named gap: no evidenced disaster-recovery/business-continuity policy for the platform side.
sections.disc_challenge: Nepal has largely solved the first two of the 'Three Delays' in maternal mortality — 57% of maternal deaths now occur inside health facilities (Nepal Maternal Mortality Study, 2021). Risk has moved upstream into the gaps between clinical visits: hypertensive disorders, anaemia/nutrition, migration-related stress, climate disruption to ANC/PNC attendance, and unverified information outpacing clinical guidance. The problem is mothers unsupported between visits, not mothers unable to reach a facility.
sections.disc_users: Pregnant and postpartum women, especially rural, low-income, low-literacy women without smartphones or reliable connectivity, who today rely on FCHVs, family elders, and informal/online advice between ANC/PNC visits. Danger signs between visits are frequently missed or acted on late. Design deliberately includes the family — content addressed to husbands/mothers-in-law after 28 weeks, since pregnancy decisions are rarely made by the mother alone.
sections.disc_stakeholders: MoHP and District Health Offices are the accountable government tier; Makwanpur District Government funded the product in its 2013/14 district plan. Clinical/academic partners: Tribhuvan University Institute of Medicine, Patan Academy of Health Sciences. International: WHO Nepal, UNICEF Nepal. Community: FCHV networks, Mothers' Groups. Open item: a measurable 'no longer a problem' definition is not yet established — no outcome data exists on beneficiaries in fifteen years; closing this is the stated 2026-2030 priority.
sections.des_arch: A mother-facing app plus a toll-free, human-staffed counselling line, consistent with the non-clinical-wellness-plus-human-triage classification named in the Governance Spine. The deliberate withholding of automated risk-score triage is an architectural decision, not an oversight.
sections.des_ux: Built around the mother's own LMP date; ANC/PNC-synchronised content in audio/video/text so literacy is not a precondition; offline-first. Content schedule (first content ~12 weeks, new content every two weeks to 28 weeks, then family-addressed content) was designed in 2012 and unchanged since — stable and user-validated, but not re-tested against a changed user base in over a decade.
sections.des_integration: Integrates with the national DHIS2-based platform for the counselling programme, with a four-tier access model. Named gap: no evidenced integration with facility-level hospital information systems, laboratory, or radiology systems — referral handoff appears to rely on the ANM's direct action rather than system-to-system exchange, consistent with the low referral-closure rate noted in Deliver.
sections.del_evidence: Reach is well-evidenced (100,000+ downloads, ~1,600 mothers engaged daily, 1,798 counselling notes Jan-Jul 2025, 48 danger-sign cases identified and referred). Outcome evidence is not: referral loop closed in only 4% of events (69 of 1,727). The 'lives potentially associated with timely referral' figure (19-20) is an explicit estimate of association, never 'lives saved.' No formal study design or cost-effectiveness metric exists yet for closing the evidence gap; it is the named 2026-2030 priority.
sections.del_scale: Budget-line precedent (Makwanpur District Government, 2013/14) and institutional licensing precedent (One Heart Worldwide, 2023) show the sustainability model has worked twice outside founder capital. Full operational handover to a government tier is not evidenced at national scale — the organisation still operates the core app and counselling line. Decision owner for closing the evidence gap and activating risk-score triage is the organisation's own 2026-2030 strategy.
sections.del_business: Free at point of use for mothers, always, held since 2012. Institutions pay: government programmes, NGO/INGO partnerships, platform licensing, health-system integration. No national health insurance reimbursement pathway is evidenced or claimed.
sections.val_equity: Strongest explicit design target: devices provided where mothers have none, zero-literacy content design, family addressed after 28 weeks. Unresolved: whether the 4% referral-closure rate is evenly distributed or concentrated among the hardest-to-reach mothers — not analysed.
sections.val_population: Reach is large and the upstream-risk framing is well-evidenced at national-statistics level. Population-level outcome attribution is the stated evidence gap.
sections.val_patient: Strong by design: offline-first, audio/video for low literacy, Nepali-language, free at point of use, a real human on a toll-free line. The product's most consistently strong aim.
sections.val_provider: FCHV/ANM tooling mirrors field workflows rather than imposing a new one, consistent with the organisation's long-held 'mirror the health worker's existing forms' principle.
sections.val_cost: Free-to-mother, institutions-pay model has two real funding precedents outside founder capital. Full cost-per-outcome is not calculable without outcome data — same gap as Population Health.
